title: India Just Ripped Up Its Tax Code for Foreign Bond Investors. A Billion Dollars Flowed In Within Three Days.
excerpt: The government scrapped withholding and capital gains taxes on foreign investments in government bonds — the most aggressive move to attract overseas capital since the crisis began. State Street calls it a 'game-changer.'
body:
India has abolished capital gains and withholding taxes on foreign investments in government bonds — a sweeping reform that produced immediate results. More than $1 billion in government debt was purchased in just three trading sessions after the announcement, compared with $1.6 billion in the entire year-to-date period before it.

The measures, unveiled on Friday of last week as part of a coordinated blitz by the government and the Reserve Bank of India, represent the most aggressive attempt to attract foreign capital since the Iran war began disrupting India's external balances in late February. The government scrapped a 12.5% long-term capital gains tax on government securities held by foreign portfolio investors, and removed a 20% withholding tax on interest earned from those bonds. Both exemptions took effect from April 1, 2026.

"We believe that these changes are a game-changer for debt flows," said Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt and systematic fixed income at State Street Investment Management, which manages about $5.6 trillion in assets.

The reforms go further than tax. The RBI broadened the pool of government securities available through the Fully Accessible Route — the channel that allows unlimited foreign investment — to include all new 15-year, 30-year and 40-year bonds. The Bank for International Settlements, an active investor in Indian government securities, was specifically exempted from all taxes.

The objective is not just short-term relief. A senior government official told Reuters that the capital gains tax removal was aimed squarely at helping India's inclusion in Bloomberg's Global Aggregate Index — the flagship benchmark that had deferred India's entry earlier this year, disappointing investors who had expected an imminent addition.

Inclusion in a global bond index would transform the nature of capital flows into India. Unlike the hot money that characterises equity portfolio investment, index-driven bond allocation tends to be passive, persistent and predictable. "This could bring consistent, predictable foreign capital inflow," a government analyst noted, adding that it would also lower India's borrowing costs over time.

The early market response has been encouraging. Yields on government bonds have fallen 10 to 30 basis points across the curve since the announcement, with shorter maturities seeing the biggest declines. The 10-year benchmark yield ended last week at 6.977%, down for the second consecutive week.

But India's Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran, speaking on Friday, cautioned against expecting similar treatment for equities. "The case for changes to capital gains taxes on equities is weaker than for bonds," he told NDTV, suggesting the government sees the bond reforms as a targeted intervention rather than the start of a broader tax overhaul.

The distinction is practical. India stands broadly in line with global standards on equity taxation, but was among the few countries that taxed non-resident flows into debt instruments. The asymmetry had long been cited by global fund managers as a barrier to meaningful allocation to Indian government bonds, even as the country's economy remained the fastest-growing among major nations.

The bond tax changes are part of a broader package designed to shore up India's external defences. The RBI announced it would bear the full hedging cost for three-to-five-year foreign currency deposits from non-resident Indians — a move that prompted banks including HDFC, SBI and AU Small Finance Bank to raise NRI deposit rates by up to 300 basis points, with some now offering as high as 7.1%. Analysts estimate these deposits alone could pull in $35-40 billion through September.

The government also eased overseas borrowing rules for banks and companies, encouraged NRI-backed lending arrangements, and signalled that capital expenditure would not be cut despite the unplanned fiscal costs of the Iran war.

For the rupee — Asia's second-worst performing currency this year, down 6% — the reforms represent a structural rather than cosmetic defence. Foreign portfolio investors have pulled nearly $30 billion from Indian equities in 2026, but the bond market is now beginning to move in the other direction.

The question is whether the inflows can match the outflows. State Street's Taylor thinks they can, at least on the debt side. "The measures should boost foreign participation across the yield curve and lower borrowing costs over time," she said.

For NRIs, the package delivers a double benefit: higher deposit rates with government-backed hedging, and a stronger case for India's inclusion in global bond indexes that would stabilise the very currency their remittances are denominated in. Whether the $1 billion in three days becomes a trend or a blip will depend on what happens next at the Strait of Hormuz — and whether the Bloomberg index committee is watching.
